definition: A feeling of guilt or unease that makes a person hesitate to do something wrong.
example: He felt a twinge of compunction after reading his sister's diary without asking.
nuance: Compunction is a pang of conscience, often felt before acting and common in negatives like "no compunction"; remorse is deeper regret felt afterward.
prompt: A student finds a wallet full of cash on the seat beside him on the bus.
options: He felt compunction at the thought of keeping the cash, so he gave the wallet to the driver.
An irresistible compunction to count the bills made him open the wallet again and again.
His compunction showed in how gleefully he spent the found cash on snacks.
The wallet's owner felt deep compunction when the driver returned it, and she thanked the student warmly.
reasons: His guilty unease about taking money that wasn't his stopped him from doing it.
An uncontrollable urge is a compulsion, a look-alike word, not a twinge of conscience.
Cheerfully spending someone else's money shows a lack of guilt, the reverse of the word's sense.
She did nothing wrong; relief and gratitude are not feelings of guilt.

practice.prompt: A baker realizes she gave a customer the wrong change earlier that morning.
options: With no compunction at all, the baker apologized tearfully and refunded the customer twice over.
Struck by compunction, the baker ran after the customer to return his missing change.
The baker felt compunction about her prize-winning loaf and proudly entered it in the county fair.
The baker's compunction meant she unlocked the shop at six sharp every single morning.
reasons: Tearful apologies show plenty of guilt, so saying she had none contradicts her actions.
Her uneasy conscience over the mistake pushed her to set it right.
Pride in good work is the opposite of a guilty conscience.
Opening on time reflects punctuality, a similar-sounding idea, not moral unease.
